transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-01-24
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Alex Monroe (Redwood AE), Priya Singh (Redwood SE), John Patel (Equinox CTO), Maya Chen (Platform Lead), Samir Rao (SRE)

Summary:
High-level intake call focused on Equinox Labs' requirement for reserved GPUs with tenant isolation, burst capability, and predictable latency for a customer-facing inference product. Discussed tradeoffs between dedicated pools and hosted fallbacks, SSO/KMS requirements, and a lightweight pilot plan.

Topics:
- Current infra and constraints
- Isolation and data residency
- Burst and prewarm strategy (hotpool, prewarmed nodes)
- Scaling expectations and autoscale policies
- Security: SOC2, SSO, KMS, audit logs
- Next steps and POC scope

Transcript: (timestamps approximate, transcription imperfect)
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Alex from Redwood, AE on this account. We'll do a quick intro, go over the high level requirements, and Priya will jump into the technical questions.
[00:12] John: Thanks Alex. I'm John, CTO here at Equinox Labs. We run a real-time inference product for recommendation and chat, roughly 200ms p50 target, p95 under 700. We explored hosted but worried about multi-tenancy noise, so want reserved GPUs.
[00:28] Priya: Great, thanks John. Quick question — are you thinking fully private deployment (VPC) or Redwood Dedicated in our hosted region with dedicated pools?
[00:36] John: Prefer dedicated pools first, we want the operational simplicity but also strict isolation. Data doesn't leave region and logs need to be sent to our Splunk.
[00:46] Maya: One thing — we need separation at the tenant level, some customers are financials so must have dedicated tenancy or strong logical isolation. Can you describe how isolation works?
[00:55] Priya: Sure. Our Dedicated offering supports reserved GPU pools that are single-tenant from a scheduling perspective. You can allocate node pools per customer segment or use namespace-level isolation with RBAC. Networking can be VPC-peered so traffic never goes through public internet. Note: some customers opt for Private when they need keystore/HSM on-prem.
[01:14] Samir: How about noisy neighbor problems, e.g., KV cache thrashing on long-context models? We saw that once in our infra.
[01:21] Priya: We do prefix caching and per-tenant KV cache partitioning for Dedicated — honestly sometimes the transcript system hears it as KV cash — but we partition the kv store and pin caches to nodes. Additionally, we recommend quantization profiles for large models to reduce memory pressure.
[01:37] John: What's the typical warmup time for a GPT-like 30B model on your infra? We run a mix of 8k and 16k contexts.
[01:45] Priya: With prewarmed pools you can get first-token latencies down to 60–120ms for the 30B-class on A100-type capacity, depending on batch sizing. Cold start varies 6–20 seconds if the kv cache and kernels need to initialize. Our hotpool option keeps a small set of pre-initialized sessions.
[02:03] Alex: Important to note — hotpools are configurable; you can reserve X prewarmed GPUs or keep a small burstable pool. That helps when you have unpredictable traffic spikes.
[02:12] Maya: For compliance — SOC2 is a must, we also need SAML SSO and KMS integration. Do you support external KMS?
[02:19] Priya: Yes, Dedicated and Private support customer-managed KMS through our KMS integrations. For Private deployments we can integrate with on-prem HSM. We ship audit logs and token-level telemetry to external sinks like Splunk or S3.
[02:32] Samir: Cost question: If we reserve for baseline and burst, how do you price burst usage? Is it on-demand or pre-bought credits?
[02:40] Alex: The model is reserved commit for baseline throughput and a burst tier that is billed at a higher rate when used. There's also an option for a hybrid contract: commit a base and prepay burst credits at a discounted rate. We'll send the SKU matrix after this call.
[02:52] John: Latency vs cost — our SLO is strict for paid customers. We need deterministic p95. How do you ensure that under heavy load?
[03:01] Priya: We recommend two tactics: 1) split traffic across dedicated pools by SLA class (e.g., premium pool pinned to lower-batch settings), and 2) implement routing with fallbacks — if primary pool is saturated we failover to a slightly cheaper or lower-precision model for degraded mode. Also autoscale policies can prefetch nodes before thresholds hit.
[03:21] Maya: Is model quantization supported? We don't want big quality regressions but need cost savings.
[03:26] Priya: Yes, we have quant profiles and per-model quality checks. For some workloads 4-bit quant can be acceptable; we also recommend eval sets to guard quality regressions — Redwood Optimize can run regression alerts on your test prompts.
[03:40] Samir: Can we do canary rollouts and A/B testing for new model versions?
[03:44] Priya: Absolutely. The Console supports canary percentages, A/B routing, and automatic fallback if error rates spike. You can pin a model to a route and roll out 5% then 20% etc.
[03:56] John: For the pilot, we want to test at our 10% peak traffic for two weeks and observe p95 and token cost. Do you have a recommended pilot scope?
[04:06] Alex: Yes — recommended pilot: 2-week POC on a dedicated pool sized for 10% peak, use hotpool size of 2 GPUs for prewarm, enable logging to your Splunk instance, and run synthetic and live traffic against a pinned model. Priya will supply the benchmark script.
[04:19] Maya: Networking — can we force egress through our NAT and have IP allowlist?
[04:24] Priya: With VPC peering we can control egress; we also support IP allowlisting for management traffic. For Private we can run entirely within your VPC.
[04:33] Samir: Any talk about maintenance windows and SLA credits?
[04:37] Alex: Dedicated SLAs include uptime and latency targets in the contract with maintenance windows — we provide runbook and a maintenance calendar. Credits apply per contract terms.
[04:46] John: One more — how fast can we scale from 10% to full production? We can anticipate a month to ramp but need to ensure no surprises.
[04:54] Priya: Autoscale policies can be configured to scale by node count and warmup thresholds. For large jumps we recommend staged scale: ramp to 50% capacity with warm prepull, then full. If you need rapid surge, burst pools can add capacity in minutes depending on quota.
[05:09] Alex: Operational note — we recommend keeping a small always-on baseline of reserved nodes so you avoid frequent cold starts; burst pools handle spikes.
[05:17] John: Understood. We will gather token distribution and traffic traces.
[05:21] Maya: What's the expected on-call support during POC?
[05:24] Alex: Standard includes business-hours support; for the POC we can provide SE standby for critical runs. If you upgrade to enterprise or a higher support tier, 24/7 on-call is available.
[05:36] Samir: We heard about model kernel selection — will you manage low-level optimizations or do we need to tune?
[05:41] Priya: Redwood's runtime auto-selects kernels, but SEs can advise model compile flags and quant profiles. We'll do a one-time tuning pass during the POC.
[05:52] John: Any blockers we should be aware of? Our main constraints are: A) strict tenant isolation, B) deterministic p95 under sudden traffic, C) KMS integrations for encrypted payloads.
[06:06] Priya: None major — isolation is supported with dedicated pools or Private if you want full control. Deterministic p95 relies on pool sizing and prewarm strategy, which we'll help define. KMS integrations work but for on-prem HSM there's some extra infra work and a longer lead time.
[06:22] Alex: OK, recap of next steps: Alex will send pricing and reserved SKU options; Priya will share prewarm/playbook and benchmark script; Maya will share traffic traces. We'll reconvene after Equinox ingests the materials to schedule the POC kickoff.
[06:37] John: Sounds good. One small note — when you send pricing, include comparative cost for full Private deployment so we can evaluate TCO.
[06:45] Alex: Will do.
[06:47] Maya: Thanks everyone.
[06:49] Alex: Thanks, we'll follow up by EOM.
